utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. As the Chamber advised the parties on 20th of August, today we are holding a Status Conference to discuss the progress of the trial to date and to hear from the parties on their views as to how the trial can be moved forward more expeditiously. As everyone is aware, before the beginning of the trial phase of this case we had a discussion about the size of the case and the consequent expected overall length of the proceedings. Prior to issuing the decision on the application of Rule 73 bis, by which we granted the Prosecution a total of 300 hours for the presentation of its evidence-in-chief, I, as Pre-Trial Judge, and the Chamber, as a whole, repeatedly emphasised the importance of ensuring that this trial is conducted fairly and expeditiously. In order to guarantee both fairness and expeditiousness, we expressed the view that the trial needs to be a manageable one, both in terms of the volume of evidence brought and the time taken, inside and outside the courtroom, to introduce and analyse that evidence, and ultimately to produce a written judgement on the charges against the accused, Mr. Karadzic. At the same time, the Chamber performed some calculations based on the 300 hours granted to the Prosecution for the presentation of its case-in-chief, and on certain assumptions founded in the experience of other Tribunal cases, to estimate when the trial might be concluded and the judgement issued. You will be aware that the rough estimate we came to at the time of the Status Conference last year was the end of December 2012 for the completion of proceedings at trial, meaning the rendering of the judgement. Having started hearing evidence in this case on 13 April 2010, the Chamber, with the assistance of the Registry, has been closely monitoring the time used in the courtroom by the parties, as well as for procedural matters, and the nature and volume of the evidence being brought. We found it necessary, in June, to begin imposing time-limits on Mr. Karadzic for his cross-examination of the witnesses being brought by the Prosecution, after repeated advice and warnings given to him that he was not using his time effectively, nor sensibly. There still remains room for improvement in terms of the manner in which the cross-examination is being conducted and the time for cross-examination with each witness, which I will address further in a moment. However, in light of the fact that almost every one of the Prosecution's witnesses is being brought under Rule 92 ter, meaning that in addition to their oral testimony, the Prosecution is regularly submitting a lengthy written statement or transcript of evidence given by them, as well as a number of associated exhibits, it is unrealistic to expect the cross-examination of these witnesses to be very short. Analysing the time reports which are prepared on a monthly basis, I should note that since the beginning of the hearing of evidence, the cross-examination has taken, on average, 350 per cent of the time spent by the Prosecution. Since the Chamber began imposing time-limits, up to the end of Mr. Blaszczyk's testimony, and not including Mr. Suljevic's evidence, for whom the accused's cross-examination has not been yet concluded, the cross-examination has taken, on average, 275 per cent of the time spent by the Prosecution. If we assume that this will not change or, for the purpose of our calculation, if we simply assume that for the remainder of the Prosecution's case Mr. Karadzic will take about 250 per cent of the time used by the Prosecution for his cross-examination, all other things being equal, the hearing of evidence would not be concluded until July 2013 on a four-day-per-week sitting schedule. That date would change to January 2013 were we to move to a five-day-per-week sitting schedule in October of this year. Moreover, we also need to factor in the time necessary for any rebuttal and rejoinder evidence, for preparation of closing briefs and arguments, and for the preparation of the judgement, which, of course, also depends on the volume of evidence to be reviewed and analysed by the Chamber. Taking an optimistic approach, this should add about six to nine months to the process following the completion of the evidence phase until the final judgement is rendered, meaning between August 2013 and April 2014, in the various scenarios I have just laid out. I'm confident in saying, however, that the volume of evidence, in terms of witness testimony and exhibits that we'll have to consider at the end of the trial, will be unprecedented at this Tribunal if we continue at the current rate, and that this may well necessitate an even longer period for the finalisation of the judgement. We've previously indicated that a trial of no more than three years' length is manageable, and we are concerned that this trial may increase in length to four or even more years, if these calculations prove accurate. While we recognise that this is, indeed, one of the largest cases before the Tribunal, and that the scope of this indictment and nature of the allegations against the accused are such that it is going to be long and complex, our primary concern is to ensure a fair and expeditious trial, and that a trial which is not manageable, in terms of its size, risks undermining these requirements. So with these introductory remarks, I would like to hear from the parties concerning the efforts that they have made and continue to make to assist us in this regard, and on whether they have specific proposals for ways in which the proceedings can be rendered more expeditious. First, I would hear from the Prosecution. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. In reviewing the testimony and, in general, the proceedings that have taken place thus far in anticipation of this conference, we were alert to the issue of identifying for the Chamber those factors about which we consider the Chamber to be most interested, and that is: how to ensure the receipt of the most appropriate relevant evidence in the most usable digestible form which the Court can assimilate, and in a manner that renders the proceedings most efficient and, ultimately, most expeditious. And one issue in particular seemed to surface repeatedly and implicate a number of the concerns of the Court and the issues it has raised, and I'll discuss that as I -- or identify those factors as I discuss this particular issue. The Court will be aware that at various points during the course of the case -- well, let me step back from that. Obviously, there are two ways in which the Court -- or two primary ways in which the Court receives evidence, and that's through witnesses and through the submission of documents. I think the Court has already addressed, to some extent, the time issues associated with witness testimony by focusing on the factors of time allocation and time percentages used. The Prosecution has endeavoured, to the maximum extent possible, to render its submission of evidence via witnesses as efficient and effective as possible through the use of those mechanisms available through the Rules of Evidence and Procedure, and most of the time consumed with witnesses on the stand has been by the accused, in part for the reasons mentioned by the Court, that is, the nature of 92 ter and its efficient manner of presentation can result in a greater length of time for cross-examination, even when used effectively; number 2, the Court has been able to identify the manner in which the accused has not necessarily used his time effectively but has, instead, used it for argumentation and for the pursuant of irrelevant inquiries. But beyond that, it seems to me, when we looked carefully at and tried to deconstruct the approach to cross-examination, a good deal of time has been consumed with the effort by the accused to ensure that the documents of interest to the Defence were admitted. And in so doing, he has attempted to find some nexus or link with those documents and the witness, no matter how tenuous, in an effort to justify the admission of those documents. And I believe the Court will be aware and I believe the Defence will be aware of many efforts to do so with many witnesses. That has been necessitated by the approach taken in response to both the Prosecution's efforts and the Defence's efforts to submit documents to the Court in another manner, and that's through Bar table submissions. I almost hesitate to raise that, because for some reason that term has come to signify something that seems to be a necessarily secondary or subordinate approach to admitting documentation, but I'd like to speak to the Court about why I think we've reached a stage in the case where that's not the case. I recall that the -- the Court's focus was, understandably, on restricting the primary use of the Bar table submissions at the outset of the case, out of concern that it would lack contextualisation, that it would result in a potential flood of documents which the Court couldn't properly assimilate, and that the burdens of dealing with that information would render the trial unmanageable. In that respect, I think the good news of the time taken thus far in the case by the accused with the cross-examinations, and the fairly cumbersome approach that may be said to have marked some of the examinations thus far, is that a huge amount of contextualisation has taken place. The accused has canvassed with many, many witnesses the breadth of the conflict, even with those who weren't really in a position to talk with any authority about particular issues raised by documents or speak to those documents, themselves. In fact, to the extent that the Court has, on more than one occasion, invited the accused specifically, and in that context I take the parties generally, to reconsider the use of Bar table submissions for documents that have clearly been contextualised by that time, either through that particular witness or by other witnesses. The advantage of that contextualisation and, therefore, the broadened opportunity for the submission of documents through Bar table submissions is considerable and, indeed, manifold. Now, I want to say from the outset that we are not referring to, and I trust that Mr. Robinson, in his earlier submissions, was also not referring to the prospect of flooding the Chamber with marginally relevant documents that the Court would not be in a position to properly assimilate. And I don't think he was talking about the submission of documents that hadn't, in some manner, been contextualised during the course of the case. But as we know, the reason documents are presented to witnesses is either for authentication, which has, for the most part, not been an issue in this case and which, for the most part, does not require witnesses, there's generally an agreement upon the authentic nature of the documents that have been proffered, or to some manner of contextualisation that enables the Court to receive the documents in a meaningful way and to apply them in a meaningful way to the issues in the case. And as I say, I believe we've reached that point, and here are some of the benefits that accrue from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before going further, I'd like to mention a comment, that the Chamber never closed the door to the possibility of receiving documents through Bar table motions. What we restricted is to introduce documents through a witness who cannot confirm anything about --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I quite agree, Your Honour. And if this seemed like some unintended criticism of the Court, that's not what was meant. In fact, it was a wake-up call to the parties to, at this stage of the case, use more fulsomely the opportunity presented for a more efficient production of information for the Court. And I think, as the Court is aware, having invited the parties now, during the course of courtroom sessions, to do so, I don't think that, with the exception of Assembly sessions, I consider that the use of Bar table submissions has not been as fulsome as the circumstances require and as, I think, the parties should endeavour to use now, and I wanted to identify some of the benefits of doing so in terms of its impact on the length of the case. Number 1, I indicated one, and that is it will almost surely reduce the time needed for cross-examination and, indeed, for direct examination. There should no longer be an effort to exhaust time in court attempting to find some link between the witness and the document, one by one, that doesn't really end up adding appreciably to the Court's understanding of the document, but provides a trigger for the admission of that document. So we'll save time in a very direct manner. Number 2, it enables -- it puts the Court, at an earlier phase in the case, in a position to better assess the relevance of testimony and the relevance of further documentation that might be submitted. So the Court can exercise its powers to contract or expand the length of examination for either direct or cross for particular witnesses, being aware of the -- more fully and more precisely the significance of the issue that's being addressed. Number 3, the parties are in a position, at an earlier phase in the case, to ensure that the documents they consider most significant have been tendered and admitted, and thereby not spend unnecessary time with witnesses attempting to get in documents that may be less significant, but which they want to see admitted as a safe-guard because they do not yet know whether the documents that more directly establish -- or they believe more directly establish the issues that are of concern to them have been admitted. That also has an impact on the assessment of not only the time that needs to be taken by upcoming witnesses, but, indeed, on the assessment of which witnesses may or may not, in fact, be required. The earlier the evidence is before the Court, and as the parties continue to assess and evaluate the totality of the evidence before the Court, they are in a better position to gauge whether witnesses need to be called, whether witnesses need to be cross-examined, the extent of time necessary for that direct examination or cross-examination, and so on. I believe there are multiple benefits that accrue from that. And I mentioned before the same thing will be true for the Court as it attempts to address issues of relevance. Thus far, the Prosecution has only sparingly made objections to evidence which it considers or at least is perilously close to implicating the issue of tu quoque, or, at best, has marginal relevance to the case. Clearly, as the case goes on and the issues become clearer and more concrete, the prospect of identifying issues that are at such a far extreme of relevance or that, indeed, have crossed the line into being tu quoque, becomes heightened, and the Prosecution will be in a position to more assertively identify areas where those occur. The Defence can respond accordingly, but the Court will be in a much better position, as it has received the information earlier, to assess the significance of areas of examination inquiry that may be too far at the outer edge or that fall into the area of tu quoque. And the final advantage I'll mention about the Bar table submissions is that, I think, as the Court indicated in its earlier decisions, the parties will be expected to clearly identify the relevance of those documents, to really focus in and explain to the Court why those documents are being presented, what their relevance is, how it's significant to the case, and how it's significant to the case at that particular point in the case. That will result in a great deal more information to the Court than can possibly be -- or that has been and I think is likely to be elicited from witnesses during the course of cross-examination. And, further, the Court will be able to assess the significance of any particular tendered document in the context of other related documents. And I think that will ultimately narrow the number of documents that are submitted to the most significant ones. So those are -- we tried to canvass the proceedings that have taken place thus far, not with any preconceptions in mind but to see what sort of issues emerged during the course of that review, and for the reasons I just described, that particular item seemed to surface repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Last year, when we decided to grant 300 hours to the Prosecution to present its case, the Chamber tried to calculate the overall length of the trial, as I mentioned earlier today, and we came to the conclusion that we would be able to deliver the judgement in this case at the end of 2012. At the time, as I also mentioned, we based our calculation on certain assumptions. Mainly, we made use of the guide-lines in the ICTY Manual on Developed Practices. Accordingly, for the cross-examination of the Prosecution's viva voce witnesses, we allocated 60 per cent of the Prosecution's estimated time for its examination-in-chief. However, there were only two viva voce witnesses, and therefore it didn't matter much at the end of the day. Of significant importance are the Rule 92 ter witnesses, the total number of which is 223. We allocated time for cross-examination by the accused of those Rule 92 ter witnesses at least equal to the time estimated by the Prosecution for their examination-in-chief. There, we may have been too optimistic. I'm now speaking for myself, but when we did that calculation, i.e., allocating to the accused for his cross-examination the same time as would be used by the Prosecution, I anticipated that most of the Rule 92 ter witnesses would be introduced, to use the ICTY jargon, as partial ter witnesses instead of as full ter witnesses. In other words, significant parts of the witness's evidence would still be led live, so that, therefore, limiting the time for cross-examination to the same time as the Prosecution would use for its examination-in-chief should be okay. However, in this regard I'm obliged to mention that the Prosecution's use of Rule 92 ter in this case is unprecedented in that for almost all their live witnesses, albeit partial in the case of Rule 92 ter witnesses, there's a significant quantity of written evidence as well as some oral testimony. But the former, the written evidence, tends to outweigh the latter, oral testimony, in terms of quantity. Moreover, for each Rule 92 ter witness, there are a number of associated exhibits being submitted by the Prosecution, which also add significantly to the volume of evidence in this case. The Chamber is concerned about the impact of such heavy reliance upon the provisions in the Rules which allow the submission of evidence in writing, plus associated exhibits, in a case of this already considerable size. So, therefore, in this regard, the question I would like to put to the witness [sic] at this moment, also given that the Prosecution is minded to use the regime of tendering a document through Bar table motion, is whether it still considers that it needs all of the originally-granted 300 hours to present its case. Or given that the Prosecution has used 41 hours so far during the past four months, whether it still needs all of its remaining time, i.e., 259 hours, to present its remaining case. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we haven't done that precise calculation in that sense as the Court is now inquiring, and, as I say, it would be just the slightly revised approach which I just discussed I think would have an impact on that. But we do know already that -- we did make some calculations -- some projections, and it's already clear that, even at this point, that the Prosecution would complete its case, based on what's happened to date and based on the projections we made, below the 300 hours. And I believe our calculations were about -- it wasn't quite 10 per cent below, but it was in that vicinity. But we -- I don't want to indicate that we undertook a new review to reconsider each and every individual witness. Instead, we made a projection of what's happened to date, based on the time that's being consumed thus far, and added that into the calculation, and, based on the time the Prosecution has used thus far, come up with a figure I just mentioned. My assessment is that the heightened use of the Bar table submission in the manner I suggested, and as I indicated as I spoke, we would certainly expect to be continually reviewing the totality of the evidence and assessing the prospective testimony of each listed witness in that light, might well result in a further reduction of the time necessary for the Prosecution's case. So, sorry for that long answer. What it means is we've already come to a point at which our projections indicate the number of hours would be at least less than the 300, more in the area of approximately 280 at this point, and I would anticipate that if we proceeded in the manner we were just discussing, that a further reduction of time would result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Another issue I would like to raise with the Prosecution is concerned with disclosure. The Chamber has found in several decisions, Mr. Tieger, that the Prosecution has violated its disclosure obligations vis-a-vis the accused, and we've expressed serious concern about those violations. The Prosecution cannot expect the trial proceedings to be conducted expeditiously if it continues to disclose material to the accused which he should have received many months before, which then results in a motion being filed by the accused, to then be decided by the Trial Chamber, all of which creates extra work and takes time and resources to deal with. More seriously, if the accused is found to be prejudiced by such late disclosure, sanctions may have to be imposed, which could further delay the proceedings. I wonder if you like to comment on this observation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning. We have implemented these additional measures. And you have given us a dead-line to meet for the 1st of October, and we are quite confident that we will meet the dead-line and these violations will not continue. That's what I would have to add to this. But I also have to say, as we always provide the details in our responses to the motions, there was so far no prejudice for the accused. And the witnesses concerned are basically witnesses that have to -- that will appear in a very late order. So, so far I think we have not delayed the trial because of these oversights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff. I take your words, and all this disclosure will be complete by the date you indicated. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to add one point, Your Honour. The Prosecution takes all of its disclosure obligations very seriously, and that's been evidenced by tremendous efforts by the Prosecution team to address and re-address and expend extraordinary time and resources to ensure, to the maximum human extent possible, that that's been accomplished. In part, I think that is reflected in the fact that if the Court looks at the kinds of materials that have surfaced from the repeated reviews and that have been the subject of the motions regarding violations, they are materials that haven't, as Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff indicated, resulted in any prejudice whatsoever. They've been quite marginal materials that fall within the -- they're not central, they don't indicate any kind of egregious oversight of the need to make those disclosures. They are matters that fall within, to some extent, the inevitable administrative oversights that occur when large amounts of material are being reviewed. And beyond that, I think the Defence is well aware of the fact that the Prosecution has been responsive to every effort for collaborative assistance. We have, I'm sure Mr. Robinson will confirm this, bent over backwards to assist the Defence where we could, where there was no requirement to do so. Mr. Robinson is aware that every good-faith effort is being made and has been made by the Prosecution. We don't want any oversights or non-disclosures to take place for any reason, whether they involve marginal or non-prejudicial materials or not, and we've engaged in unprecedented efforts to prevent that from happening. And I just mention that because I don't want the kinds of occasional and almost inevitable oversights that have taken place in every case that's occurred in the Prosecution -- in the Tribunal's history thus far to be elevated into something it's not. We are doing everything humanly possible and will continue to do so proactively to ensure the most efficient possible trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, I expect the Prosecution to meet the dead-line we gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Now I give the floor to Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. Good morning to all. The Defence also believes that this conference was truly indispensable, even more so after we've heard the introductory analysis presented by His Excellency Mr. Kwon. The Defence waited for this kind of opportunity to arise so that we did not deal with these questions when examining witnesses. I believe that I have already said that this system, this legal system, is new and unusual for us, because all of that is different in our part of the world, procedural law and legislation, as such. However, what is done in the Tribunal is new and unusual when compared to any system. For example, we have 223 witnesses here according to 92 bis -- sorry, 92 ter. Also, there was an enormous number of 92 bis witnesses that had been envisaged. Some will remain 92 bis witnesses, but thanks to the ruling of the Trial Chamber, some of them have turned into 92 ter witnesses. Also, there are going to be some 92 quater witnesses. There are going to be witnesses who've never appeared here, who will never appear here, who are never cross-examined by any Defence team, and whose statements will, nevertheless, become part of the evidence of this case. 223 witnesses are going to speak briefly. We will not be able to catch them out, in terms of the inconsistency in relation to what they had stated earlier on, because they will not be making statements here, they will simply stand by the statements that they had made before that. There will be some witnesses who can only be cross-examined by God Almighty because they've passed away in the meantime. If my math is right, I think there are about 170 protected witnesses. Almost none of them are victims, so protective measures are absolutely unjustified. Moreover, there is a vast amount of adjudicated facts here, and the Defence has to fight against them. We have to fight to correct elementary facts that any elementary school student in our country knows. So perhaps the distinguished Mr. Tieger may think that this is irrelevant, but it is relevant. Had things been done properly so far, we would not have this situation when I have to correct, say, one adjudicated fact that the OTP sent to me recently, namely, that Yugoslavia was restored in 1945 as a republic consisting of six republics and two provinces. That is simply not correct. These two provinces became constituent elements of the federation, whatever that may mean - this is a political trap - only in 1974, by the Constitution of 1974. However, what is at stake here is showing what the sins of the Serbs were, or, rather, that the Serb Communists wanted to make the Communist Party a unitarian one in 1990. I have no sympathy for the Communists. They were my greatest enemies and opponents. But that is simply incorrect. They wanted to keep at least a semblance of federalism, whereas Croatian and Slovenian Communists wanted to destroy even this semblance of federalism. So these are things that are being built into the very foundation of this indictment, and I have to challenge that at every opportunity that I'm given, because if we look at these adjudications from other trials, even school children could laugh at that, that is so incorrect. Also, there is a great deal of associated exhibits that are brought in through witnesses. Also, there are attempts to speed up these proceedings and to scale them down by decreasing the time for examination-in-chief, and that doesn't assist the Defence at all. It actually increases the burden placed on the Defence. We have even more obligations to fight against these windmills, as it were. We have to prove things that otherwise wouldn't have to be proven. All these measures aimed at economising in terms of time, increasing efficiency, making documents more acceptable, as it were, all of this that was proposed by the OTP actually works to the detriment of the accused and the Defence. It doesn't harm them in any way. The distinguished Mr. Tieger is accusing the accused today. It's not only the indictment that is charging the accused with this and that, but also he is saying that we did other things wrongly. An accused person is there in order to be accused, but this is so wrong the Defence has to make additional efforts because these proceedings has an ongoing problem, and that is lack of evidence. Excellencies, let's see what the point of these proceedings is. Is it to find the accused guilty at any cost or to establish what it was that had actually happened there? If the point is to find the accused guilty at any cost, have them bring five documents. What do they need 40.000 documents for? Let them bring in five documents that are relevant, and that will be it. If the point is to establish what it was that had happened there, and that is what I recommend, because otherwise there is not going to be reconciliation or any kind of life there, then what should be done is to revise everything that was established in such a distorted way in other proceedings. Let's see what could have been avoided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Today we are exploring the way in which way the conduct of the proceedings could be moved forward more expeditiously. This is not the place to touch upon the merit. The example of the history or the name of the region is a good example. I waited, but to make an observation of your conduct of cross-examination, that you are needlessly using time making comments, asking questions that are irrelevant, or asking questions that witnesses clearly are unable to answer, or reading out passages from documents. I find there will be much room for further improvement, so I would like to hear from you. How would you respond to these observations?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, I agree that perhaps I did a bit too much reading, in terms of paragraphs from specific documents, that is. However, when we look at viva voce witnesses, I have no other way of proving that a witness doesn't know something or that a witness is insincere. There is no other way of handling this but putting to the witness facts that are totally opposite to what he had been saying. Also, I think that this enormous number of adjudicated facts bring me -- brings me into a position to put questions that are only seemingly irrelevant. They just seem irrelevant because they are intended to show that what had been established earlier on was totally distorted and wrong. Perhaps I'll try not to read out so many passages, or not read them out at all. But what do I do with a witness who comes here with an enormous number of documents and a very short statement? How do I make things perfectly clear in relation to this witness? How do I show that witness's credibility and competency? There is no credibility; there is no competency, then. I cannot understand that the OTP can give an enormous number of associated exhibits through a witness and I cannot ask the witness about phenomena that this witness has to know about. I have a document that proves that things were completely different, and we have to hear from the witness what he says about that kind of document. We understand the concern of the Trial Chamber about this, but please understand my concern: This is turning into a paper trial. The distinguished Mr. Tieger is saying that it's going to be very advantageous if we present more documents without witnesses, as it were. That is only working to the detriment of the Defence and the accused. Is there anything that we can do about these proceedings that would be beneficial for the accused pro reux [phoen]. Changes should be pro reux as well, not only working in favour of the OTP. I'm pleased that the distinguished Mr. Tieger finally noticed that we are talking about a vast amount of material. However, it is even bigger, it is even more huge, as it were, for the Defence, and the Defence has far less resources. I will do my very best in the future not to read. However, please, can the Prosecution not say what is important for the Defence? They said what is important for them. The Defence knows. I have well-timed questions, and what I have in mind is something that had already been adjudicated, so if I'm asking a witness to respond to something that may seem irrelevant at a given point in time, it is, believe me, highly relevant. Trust me, this trial is going to be very important in history because of its precedence, because of the way in which a people and its leadership were treated. This is a basis for all further proceedings, primarily for presidents of entities and states and for civilian heads of state and army chiefs. If we lay the wrong kind of foundations now, it's not only that the Serbs are going to be prejudiced; also, our neighbours, who are going to continue believing that the Serbs are wrong, say Markale. Very soon, professional circles are going to examine what it was that had actually happened. I can understand that the Prosecution is under pressure. They don't have evidence; that's their problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I agree that this trial is very important. However, what is important, in terms of your Defence, is your defence against the charges in the indictment. This is a criminal trial. We are not pursuing to produce a white book in history or to correct the history, so I now expect you to concentrate on your defence in relation to the relevant charges of the indictment. Having said that, give me a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And also what the President, Judge Kwon, has said about the necessity for concentrating on the indictment, that applies, of course, to both sides, the indictment that the Prosecution pursues and the indictment that the defendant has to defend himself against. We have to bear in mind, of course, that the burden of proving the case lies upon the Prosecution. The defendant does not have to prove his innocence. He's simply testing the Prosecution case. While it is inevitable, in a case of this nature, that some political territory is explored, I would urge the defendant to reduce that to an absolute practical working minimum and only explore it where it is relevant and parallel to the indictment. I think we all thank the parties for their engaging with us in an attempt to reduce the length of the trial, and hope that the methodology mentioned by Mr. Tieger and appreciated, no doubt, by the Defence, will achieve that aim. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have anything to add to what you said in relation to the manner and method in which the trial proceedings should be moved on more expeditiously?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask Mr. Robinson to discuss the legal aspect. I just want to add this, however: If this were to be limited only to my responsibility, to my indictment, it would be much easier, but then why would the Prosecution need such a number of adjudicated facts, which create a framework within which every Serb is guilty, and the president the most? If they consider that to be unimportant, then they can withdraw these adjudicated facts and we can establish the facts here. Otherwise, I'm in a situation where a vast number of facts are already adjudicated, a large number of witnesses have already been admitted, they will not appear, a large number of witnesses are having protective measures. So there's a large number of questions here that are already defined. I cannot stick only to the indictment. I need to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I had to intervene again. I'm confident not a single passage of the adjudicated facts said that all Serbs are guilty at all. That's a misleading statement. Again, I emphasise that you need to concentrate on your defence against the charges in the indictment. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If I could just make a few small observations. First of all, I think historically the Tribunal has been overly optimistic in its calculations about the length of trials and are frequently going to the Security Council and explaining that they've under-calculated, and I fear that we are doing that also here. On my own calculations, which I agree can also be rough, show that the Prosecution has so far, in the four months that we have had, completed about 14 per cent of its case. So if you multiply that times 7, that's 28 months for the Prosecution's case, and that takes us to about August of 2012. Given a few months before the Defence case starts and an equal amount of time for the Defence, it would take us to February of 2015 before the case -- the evidence is completed, and time after that would be needed for judgement. Now, those may be subject also to variables, such as reduction in the Prosecution's case or the fact that the Prosecution wouldn't need as much time to cross-examine our witnesses as we've needed to do cross-examine theirs, but I know that in business people tend to plan for the worst-case scenario as opposed to planning for the best-case scenario, and it might be wise to consider that the case could last considerably longer even than your projections are today. The other thing I would like to point out is I think that calculating between four and five days a week is not necessarily indicative of the time the trial would take, because it's very difficult to achieve a five-day week on a regular basis. Even those trials that are scheduled to sit for five days a week frequently don't, for reasons of witness availability and availability of the parties and the judges, so I don't think looking between six months difference between a four- and a five-day week necessarily would actually translate in reality to that kind of savings, and it could actually be a false economy, given the impact on the health of the accused by increasing his workload. So I would like to suggest to the Chamber that it might wish, if it really wants to make an effort to -- if it feels that the trial needs to be shorter, significantly shorter, that it revisit the idea of the scope of the indictment, which is a point we made back when they were approving the amended indictment, when the Pre-Trial Chamber was headed by Judge Bonomy. It may be that the scope of the indictment in this case is just simply too big for a manageable trial, if the Trial Chamber is concerned about the length of the trial and the impact on the fairness of the proceedings, as well as the patience of the donors to this Tribunal, and it may well be that the Chamber could revisit whether it's necessary for the Prosecution to present all of the components of its case. For example, if you were to eliminate, under Rule 73 bis (D), the municipalities portion of the case, you could probably save one year of the length of the trial, both from the Prosecution's case and the Defence case. And if you think that the Sarajevo part of the case has been difficult, I can assure you that when we start dealing with the events of 20 different municipalities, and many different events in each municipality, the unwieldiness of the trial is going to become even more apparent. And so while Mr. Tieger's suggestion of expediting the work of exhibits, and the Trial Chamber's consideration of having the improvement of Dr. Karadzic's cross-examination and its efficiency, can be implemented, those things are like pouring a small drop of water on a fire. And if the length of the trial is actually so unmanageable, in the eyes of the Chamber, it's going to take more than that in order to change the time that we finally finish this trial. And I think the Chamber ought to give consideration to more radical measures which could actually have a significant impact on the length of the trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. The figures that Mr. Robinson has cited do not conform to our calculations about the time that the Prosecution case would conclude. I think we're as much as a year off or so, and that may be based on extrapolations from the most expansive part of the case at the beginning, which does not incorporate the more efficient manner of proceeding that I think we have moved toward and will be continuing moving toward. But, in any event, no matter how you calculate them, they're quite far off from our assessment, which is much closer to, I think, an earlier figure cited by the Court, and which should be improved upon, and we'll endeavor to do so. But we don't share in any way his assessment of the projection of trial. In terms of the projected length of the Defence case, one of the reasons the case has taken as long thus far is the accused is putting forth his Defence case through Prosecution witnesses, and the Court has to be aware of that. This is not simply a matter of testing the Prosecution evidence, as His Honour Judge Morrison has observed. This is an affirmative effort, which is obviously permitted to some extent under 90(H), to adduce evidence that the accused wants to use, often which is entirely unrelated to that particular witness, as the Court must be aware and as we've seen repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is a bit premature to discuss the length of Defence case, but we issued our ruling that the Defence would have 300 hours, as the Prosecution did, to present its case. How much time you will use for your cross-examination is a separate matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the final thing I'll mention, Your Honour, is that to the extent the encouragement to eliminate some portions of the Prosecution's case, to simply eviscerate the indictment with respect to large areas of the accused's alleged criminal responsibility because of some issue of time cited by the Defence, seems at least inappropriate to me, in light of the fact that we're in this position because the accused was not available to have his case tried for so many years. And to invoke that circumstance in favour of an avoidance of the adjudication of criminal responsibility does not seem at all appropriate. But more to the point, we are moving toward, continually, a refined, expeditious process which will bring us to a conclusion at an earlier date than the dire projections cited by Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll consider all these submissions by the parties. Mr. Tieger, there's another matter which I wish to clarify. That is, in fact, connected to the issue of the overall volume of evidence in this case. In the pre-trial phase of the case of the Prosecution -- in the pre-trial phase, the Prosecution filed a number of motions for the admission of written evidence from over 150 witnesses, pursuant to Rule 92 bis. As Mr. Karadzic indicated, the Chamber issued its decision on these motions, admitting some of these witnesses' evidence under Rule 92 bis, along with relevant exhibits, but in other cases requiring the relevant witnesses to be brought for cross-examination. In such cases, I mean the witnesses coming pursuant to Rule 92 ter, the witnesses are, therefore, subject to the provisions of the Rules, i.e., Rule 92 ter. In accordance with our order on the procedure for the conduct of the trial, the Prosecution may tender only one statement or transcript of prior testimony for each such Rule 92 ter witnesses, which may mean that it needs to choose between various statements or transcripts of evidence previously given by that witness or it may need to prepare an amalgamated statement. So to avoid any possible confusion, the parties should ensure that they treat all Rule 92 ter witnesses in the same way, whether or not they were originally proposed under Rule 92 bis. Therefore, in relation to any of the witnesses originally proposed under Rule 92 bis who must come for cross-examination pursuant to Rule 92 ter, the Prosecution should carefully select which transcript or statement to tender for each witness, and which of the associated exhibits it considers necessary for admission in this case. Therefore, it should notify the accused and the Chamber so that the accused can plan his cross-examination and the Chamber can assess what is a reasonable time for cross-examination in accordance with its established procedure. Do you find any problem in my suggestion? But what I said was a ruling which was given earlier on already.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate the opportunity, Your Honour, to at least respond to any issues that may arise from this clarification of the earlier ruling. And if the Court will give us an opportunity to consider that, we will get back to the Court as soon as possible in response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. There are a couple of matters I'd like to deal with in private session in relation to binding order motions. So shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, you raised the issue of sitting schedule, whether we should sit four days a week or five days a week. We are currently sitting on a four-day-per-week schedule, which has been confirmed by the Appeals Chamber as being consonant with protection of the rights of the accused. For practical reasons, reasons of courtroom and judicial availability, we cannot move to a five-day-per-week schedule until, I must say, the end of October. In any case, should you wish to argue that this would violate his right in some way if we are to sit a five-day-per-week schedule from November, so I would encourage you -- or I would request you to make a written motion to that effect. Before closing the -- before adjourning the proceedings today, I'd like to comment on the two issues raised during the discussion with the Prosecution. The first relates to the disclosure. I appreciate the Prosecution taking additional measures to resolve the problem. However, it does not change the situation that disclosure violation had already occurred in the first place. So, in any event, I expect that by that additional measure, all the relevant material would be disclosed by 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do understand the Court's position. As I said from the outset, my comments were not intended in any way to suggest that the Prosecution didn't take its obligations under the Rules extremely seriously, and, as I say, has been expending what I believe to be unprecedented efforts to ensure that. What I was trying to say is that those Rules are imposed in an effort to ensure that the information gets to the Court, gets to the parties, in as timely a manner as possible to ensure, to the extent, the efficient management of the trial. They didn't exist in that form at the beginning. And I wanted to underscore the fact that the efforts undertaken thus far and that will continue to be made, I think, have ensured that the Chamber and the parties have been in a position to move forward as quickly as we can and manage the information as well as possible. My point was that we will continue to do so, but not to -- not to use this as a lever by either party, either to not follow through on its obligations or to overstate the significance of any deviations from the good-faith efforts -- not the good-faith efforts, any deviations in the technical possibilities available for that compliance. Everything humanly possible is being done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. The final point I'd like to raise relates to the Bar table motion you referred to. As I indicated, in response to your submission, the Chamber has not closed off the option of the parties submitting the documents from the Bar table motion. Should the parties wish to tender the document through Bar table motion, they should file a motion, a motion to that effect. But what I would like to emphasise is you should understand that any Bar table motion must explain, clearly and in detail for each particular document being offered, the relevance of the document to specific issues in the case, and how that document fits into their case, as a whole, and other evidence in the case. So, for example, if those documents which would simply -- count of the document is not sufficient to be tendered through Bar table motion. Also, it must be clear to us that the Bar table motion is not being used, as you indicated, in a broad brush way to get in huge volumes of material that may not be absolutely necessary. So please bear that in mind in the future in tendering documents through Bar table motion. I mean both parties, both the Prosecution and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll be very happy to do so, Your Honour. And I believe that in so doing, that really will help these proceedings, in effect, cut to the chase. I think the issues will become clearer and clearer, and the parties' and the Court's grasp of what remains in controversy will be that much more evident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are there any matters to raise at the moment, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have one brief matter. I don't like to say this, because the personnel who is taking care of my electronic installation is doing their best. However, I must say that I have great difficulties with electronic devices. We already by now have 2 million pages and hundreds and hundreds of audio and video material, and the software and the hardware are weak and cannot keep up with the demands. If we add -- and I would like to make some charges to the Prosecution. The cassettes are not formatised, and they're not numbered the same in the index and on the actual tapes. So now that I have been given the Mladic cassettes to listen to, I have been given two weeks, but this is not enough. Some other accused received four weeks' time. Perhaps people can read at different speeds, but you cannot listen at different speeds. So I would like to ask for an upgrading of my technical devices, because there are some unnecessary limitations imposed upon a man who is still technically innocent. I am capable of dealing with the tasks, but the limitations are there. I'm not able to use the cassettes or boxes in order to pass my comments back to Mr. Robinson and for him to be able to send his back to me. So sometimes I'm idle for two days because of these technical matters. I would kindly like to ask for some upgrades in this process and to design them in such a way that they're not always to the detriment of the Defence. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will look into the matter. But, first of all, I have to say that those are matters you have to raise with the Registry people, first of all. As I said to you, I will look into the matter and, if necessary, hear from the Registry, pursuant to Rule 33(B). Well, I think that concludes the hearing. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, excuse me for one very minor matter, but I've been asked to inform you that Exhibit D459, which had MFI status, has now received the translation up-loaded into e-court, and we ask you that you order that that document be admitted as a full exhibit. That's D459. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a look and give our ruling later on. So thank you. I thank everyone. So we trust everyone will reflect upon our discussion today and the concerns that we have raised. The Chamber will continue to monitor progress in the case to determine whether measures need to be taken in this regard. The proceedings are now adjourned until Monday next week, 6th September 2010, at 9.00 in the morning, when we will continue with the hearing of evidence. I take it that we'll hear the remaining cross-examination of Mr. Suljevic. The hearing is now adjourned.
